report:
Conclusion: the claim is **plausibly true, but modest and context-dependent**. The best evidence is not that “fresh air” is magic; it is that better bedroom ventilation lowers overnight CO₂ and sometimes improves measured or perceived sleep and next-day alertness.

A controlled bedroom study found lower CO₂ was associated with significantly better objective sleep quality, perceived air freshness, less next-day sleepiness, better concentration, and improved logical-thinking performance: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/. A small field study of 17 healthy young adults tested open window or internal door versus closed conditions and linked opening-mediated ventilation with lower bedroom CO₂ and improved sleep-quality outcomes: https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/windowdoor-opening-mediated-bedroom-ventilation-and-its-impact-on/. A later Danish study/news summary likewise reported that better bedroom ventilation improved sleep and next-day performance: https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day. A 2022 field intervention concluded outdoor-air ventilation improved bedroom indoor air quality and sleep quality: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605.

Caveats: studies are small/short-term, often in healthy young adults or specific climates, and “open window” can backfire with noise, cold drafts, pollen, wildfire smoke, urban pollution, humidity, or security concerns. An open internal door may help CO₂ but can conflict with fire-safety advice to sleep with doors closed; prioritize working smoke alarms and local fire guidance. Practical takeaway: ventilate the bedroom when outdoor air is clean and quiet—via window, door gap, mechanical ventilation, or airing before bed—while keeping temperature cool and comfortable.
